terms.def: A rechargeable battery that stores a large amount of electrical energy, such as a 12-volt car battery.
terms.more: Without internal protection, shorting the terminals can cause burns, fire, or an explosion. Charging or discharging too rapidly can cause overheating or out-gassing.

terms.def: An unintended direct path between two points of a circuit, such as a piece of metal across both battery terminals, that lets a very large current flow.
terms.more: Shorting the terminals of a 12-volt storage battery can cause burns, fire, or an explosion.

terms.def: The release of gas from a battery.
terms.more: Overheating or out-gassing is the hazard when an unprotected battery is charged or discharged rapidly. The gas may be flammable.

terms.def: What happens when electrical current flows through the body.
terms.more: Current in the body may heat tissue, disrupt the electrical functions of cells and cause involuntary muscle contractions. Guard against it with grounding and by discharging capacitors.

terms.def: The flow of electricity through a wire, a part or a body. It is measured in amperes (amps).
terms.more: Current through the body is what injures. Too much current in a circuit overheats wiring and can start a fire, which is why a fuse must have the correct ampere rating.

terms.def: The electrical pressure that pushes current through a circuit. It is measured in volts.
terms.more: US household power is 120 volts AC. High voltage can remain in equipment after it is switched off, and a meter and its leads must be rated for the voltage being measured.

terms.def: Alternating current: electricity that reverses direction many times a second, the kind supplied by wall outlets.
terms.more: US outlets supply 120 V AC through three wires: hot, neutral and ground. Use three-wire cords and plugs for all AC powered equipment.

terms.def: The wire in an AC power cable that carries the voltage from the supply. It can shock you.
terms.more: In a US three-wire 120 V AC cable, black insulation marks the hot wire. A fuse or circuit breaker goes in series with the hot conductor only.

terms.def: A safety part containing a thin piece of metal that melts and breaks the circuit when too much current flows.
terms.more: Its purpose is to remove power in case of an overload. It does not prevent shocks. Never replace a fuse with a higher-rated one: excessive current could cause a fire.

terms.def: A switch that opens by itself to cut off power when too much current flows, and can be reset afterwards.
terms.more: Like a fuse, in a 120 V AC power circuit it is installed in series with the hot conductor only.

terms.def: A condition in which more current flows in a circuit than its wires and parts are built to carry.
terms.more: An overload overheats the circuit and can cause a fire. A fuse of the correct rating removes power when it happens.

terms.def: A connection in which parts are joined end to end, so that all the current passes through each one in turn.
terms.more: A fuse or circuit breaker must be in series with the hot conductor, so that when it opens the current stops. A part connected in parallel sits beside the path and cannot interrupt it.

terms.def: A power cord with a third wire that connects the metal case of the equipment to ground.
terms.more: Using three-wire cords and plugs for all AC powered equipment is one way to guard against electrical shock.

terms.def: A connection that ties the metal cases of equipment to ground so that a fault does not leave a case live.
terms.more: Connect all AC powered station equipment to a common safety ground to guard against shock. In US wiring the ground wire is green or bare.

terms.def: A part that stores electrical charge.
terms.more: Filter capacitors in a power supply can hold a dangerous charge after it is turned off. Make sure all high-voltage capacitors are fully discharged before working inside equipment.

terms.def: Equipment that changes household AC power into the voltage a radio or other device needs.
terms.more: Immediately after it is turned off, charge stored in its filter capacitors is still a shock hazard.

terms.def: An instrument that measures voltage.
terms.more: When measuring high voltages, make sure the voltmeter and its leads are rated for use at the voltages being measured.

terms.def: A device fitted in a feed line to divert a lightning surge to ground before it reaches the station.
terms.more: Install it on a grounded panel near where the feed lines enter the building.

terms.def: The cable that carries radio signals between a radio and its antenna. Coaxial cable (coax) is a common kind.
terms.more: Lightning can travel along it into the building, so a lightning arrester is installed on a grounded panel near where feed lines enter.

terms.def: The grounding and devices that give lightning a path to earth, to reduce the danger to people, buildings and equipment.
terms.more: Ground connections must be short and direct, and sharp bends must be avoided. Lightning remains dangerous even with protection in place.

terms.def: Connecting equipment or a structure to the earth with a conductor, for electrical and lightning safety.
terms.more: Keep lightning ground wires short and direct with no sharp bends. Bond all grounds together. Local electrical codes set the grounding requirements for a tower or antenna.

terms.def: A metal rod driven into the soil to make an electrical connection to the earth.
terms.more: All external ground rods must be bonded together with heavy wire or conductive strap. A tower needs separate eight-foot rods for each leg, bonded to the tower and each other.

terms.def: Joining ground rods, earth connections or metal structures together with heavy wire or conductive strap.
terms.more: All external ground rods or earth connections should be bonded together. Tower ground rods are bonded to the tower and to each other.

terms.def: The electrical safety rules that apply where you live.
terms.more: Local electrical codes establish the grounding requirements for an amateur radio tower or antenna. FCC Part 97 does not.

terms.def: A tall structure that holds antennas high above the ground.
terms.more: Hazards include falls, contact with power lines and lightning. Climb only with training, an approved harness, tie-off at all times, and a helper or observer.

terms.def: Safety gear worn by a tower climber and attached to the tower to stop a fall.
terms.more: Tower climbing requires all three: sufficient training on safe climbing techniques, appropriate tie-off to the tower at all times, and always wearing an approved climbing harness.

terms.def: A person who stays on the ground while someone climbs a tower, to watch, assist and call for help.
terms.more: It is never safe to climb a tower without a helper or observer, whatever the height or the kind of work.

terms.def: An electrical supply wire strung above the ground. Contact with one can kill.
terms.more: Look for and stay clear of overhead wires when putting up a tower. Allow enough distance that if the antenna falls, no part of it can come within 10 feet of the power wires.

terms.def: A pole that carries power and other utility wires.
terms.more: Never attach an antenna to one: the antenna could contact high-voltage power lines.

terms.def: A tensioned cable running from a tower or mast to an anchor in the ground to hold the structure steady.
terms.more: Guy lines are tightened with turnbuckles, which need a safety wire to keep them from loosening.

terms.def: A threaded fitting that is turned to tighten a guy line.
terms.more: A safety wire is passed through it to prevent loosening of the turnbuckle from vibration. The safety wire is not there to hold the guy line if the turnbuckle breaks.

terms.def: A tower made of sections that slide inside each other so it can be raised and lowered.
terms.more: It must not be climbed unless it is retracted, or mechanical safety locking devices have been installed.

terms.def: The part of a station that sends radio signals out into the air and picks them up.
terms.more: Keep antennas well clear of power lines. Touching one during a transmission can cause an RF burn. Relocating antennas away from people reduces RF exposure.

terms.def: Radio frequency: the energy of radio signals.
terms.more: RF is non-ionizing radiation. It is not perfectly safe: strong RF heats body tissue and can burn, which is why exposure limits exist.

terms.def: Radiation that does not have enough energy to strip electrons from atoms. Radio signals are this type.
terms.more: RF does not have sufficient energy to cause chemical changes in cells and damage DNA. It can still injure by heating the body.

terms.def: Radiation with enough energy to strip electrons from atoms, such as that from radioactive material.
terms.more: It can cause chemical changes in cells and damage DNA. Radio signals are not ionizing radiation.

terms.def: The amount of radio frequency energy that reaches a person's body.
terms.more: It depends on the frequency and power level of the RF field, the distance from the antenna and the antenna's radiation pattern. Duty cycle affects the average exposure.

terms.def: Maximum permissible exposure: the limit on the strength of RF energy that people may be exposed to.
terms.more: Limits vary with frequency because the body absorbs more RF energy at some frequencies than others. Of 3.5, 50, 440 and 1296 MHz, 50 MHz has the lowest limit.

terms.def: How many times a second a radio wave completes a cycle, measured in hertz. One megahertz (MHz) is one million hertz.
terms.more: Frequency is one of the factors in RF exposure. Exposure limits vary with it because the body absorbs more RF energy at some frequencies than at others.

terms.def: A measure of how strong an RF field is at a given place: the amount of radio power passing through a given area.
terms.more: RF limits are based on the average over time. If duty cycle drops from 100 percent to 50 percent, the allowable power density increases by a factor of 2.

terms.def: The percentage of time that a transmitter is transmitting.
terms.more: It affects the average exposure to RF radiation. A lower duty cycle means lower average exposure: going from 100 to 50 percent raises the allowable power density by a factor of 2.

terms.def: The period of time over which RF exposure is averaged when checking it against the limits.
terms.more: Duty cycle is the percentage of the averaging time during which the transmitter is transmitting.

terms.def: A description of how strongly an antenna sends its signal in each direction.
terms.more: It is one of the factors that affect the RF exposure of people near an antenna, along with frequency, power level and distance.

terms.def: A check that the RF energy from your station stays within the FCC exposure limits for people.
terms.more: Acceptable methods: calculation based on FCC OET Bulletin 65, computer modeling, or measuring field strength with calibrated equipment. Re-evaluate whenever the transmitter or antenna system changes.

terms.def: A burn to the skin caused by radio frequency energy.
terms.more: Touching an antenna during a transmission can cause one. Never touch an antenna that is transmitting.

terms.def: The part of a station that produces the radio signal sent to the antenna.
terms.more: Duty cycle is the percentage of time it is transmitting. Re-evaluate RF exposure whenever an item in the transmitter or antenna system is changed.

terms.def: The person who holds the license for an amateur station.
terms.more: The station licensee is responsible for ensuring that no person is exposed to RF energy above the FCC exposure limits.

terms.def: Federal Communications Commission: the US government agency that regulates radio, including amateur radio.
terms.more: It sets the RF exposure limits, but the station licensee must make sure the station meets them. It does not set tower grounding requirements; local electrical codes do.
